title: The Assessment Illusion
author: Nick Hart
summary: Framed around the red pill scene in The Matrix, Nick Hart offers a series of deliberately provocative claims challenging the validity of the judgements schools routinely make about learning, teaching and school quality. He argues that broad termly teacher-assessment bands are too coarse to be meaningful, that 'greater depth' labels quietly lower expectations for everyone else, that standardised test scores say little about whether the curriculum has been learned, and that lesson observation and workbook scrutiny cannot reliably judge teaching or learning. Rather than evaluating, he proposes that schools build knowledge around narrowly specified problems, such as whether every Year 2 child reads at 90 words per minute or how Year 5 teachers respond to run-on sentences. He ends by arguing that accountability should move upstream, holding teachers and leaders to account first for what they choose to attend to: the specific problem, the evidence for it, the chosen and discarded strategies, and the implementation plan.
points: Hart contends that three-band teacher assessments are too broad to be valid and that the 'greater depth' category implicitly lowers the expectation for all other pupils.
He argues that small movements in standardised scores are more likely statistical noise than progress, and that progress itself cannot be measured in the way schools attempt.
Lesson observations and workbook scrutiny are presented as tools that reveal what observers like or what standards teachers accept, not what pupils have learned.
Instead of broad evaluation, he recommends building knowledge around tightly defined problems, such as specific times-table fluency or modelling of the sentence in Year 1.
Accountability, he argues, should shift upstream so leaders justify their chosen problems, evidence, strategies and implementation before being judged on impact.
quotes: Termly teacher assessments using broad categories like working towards / expected / greater depth are not valid judgements of what children have learned. They are too broad to capture meaningful information.

Greater depth’ teacher assessments can only mean that children have learned more of what was intended than those at ‘expected’. The very existence of that label quietly lowers expectations of what all children are meant to learn.
Judging writing attainment against criteria is too unreliable. Use comparative judgement for summative assessment.
Workbook scrutiny does not tell us what children have learned. It can only tell us the standard of work, effort and presentation that teachers accept.

Instead of judging or evaluating, we might just be better off seeking to build knowledge. But the complexity of school life is such that seeking to build knowledge of the teaching of reading, or writing, or maths for example is just too big.
This is where a shift is needed. If the assessments that we carry out are unreliable and the judgements invalid, perhaps holding teachers and leaders to account needs to be moved upstream a bit.

Yes, we need to be held to account on the impact of our work but if we’re paying attention to the wrong things, that impact is less likely anyway. Maybe we need to be held to account on what we decide to pay attention to first.
